findings.title: Free tokens for sale: How fake signups drive AI fraud (Okta Threat Intelligence)
findings.summary_md: Okta Threat Intelligence researchers Jeremy Kirk and Mathew Woodyard published the first part of this research on August 4, 2026, documenting gray-market AI access services including Poison Claude, which resells Anthropic model access at 5-15 percent of official token prices using the US$100 AWS Bedrock bonus credit. An exposed unauthenticated /api/status route showed Poison Claude had 881 total and 872 active users, and a companion service Ecomagent.in claimed startup-credit-funded access to Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.6 and GPT Codex 5.5. Okta notified Cloudflare and Anthropic before publication, and Cloudflare placed a phishing warning in front of poison-claude.bitsender[.]top.

findings.title: Poison Claude Sells Discounted Claude Access While Its Operator Sees Every Customer Prompt
findings.summary_md: The Hacker News covered the Okta research on August 5, 2026, listing more than half a dozen underground services advertising illegal access to AI models, with Poison Claude provisioning customers an Anthropic-compatible API key and instructing them to redirect Claude Code via environment variables. The report noted the service's api.claudeopus[.]shop status endpoint leaked user counts (881 total, 872 active), that gateway-proxy configuration gives the operator full visibility into customer prompts, and that Ecomagent.in claimed roughly 970 users.

findings.title: Token Jacking: Cybercriminals Could Be Stealing Your AI Resources (Unit 42)
findings.summary_md: Unit 42 published this telemetry report on August 6, 2026, describing incident response cases where stolen or exposed AI API keys were integrated into gray-market transfer stations within minutes, generating nearly one million dollars in charges before discovery. It traces the demand side to proxy platforms built on the open-source new-api and one-api projects, flags npm supply chain campaigns such as Shai-Hulud and Miasma as credential sources, and publishes IoCs including the Go-http-client/2.0 user agent, malicious login source IPs, and transfer-station domains amutes[.]com and abb1[.]life.

findings.title: Anthropic warns infostealer malware is hijacking Claude sessions to drain usage
findings.summary_md: BleepingComputer reported on August 30, 2026 that Anthropic began emailing Claude users whose active sessions were stolen by infostealers and drained by attackers, naming Vidar, LummaC2, StealC, RedLine and Acreed on Windows plus Atomic Stealer (AMOS) on a small number of Macs. Anthropic revoked compromised sessions, removed saved payment methods and refunded charges it identified as unauthorized, and warned that signing users out does not remove the malware. One affected user traced the infection to a pirated game download.

findings.title: Attacker stole a METR API key, used $600K worth of credits, and no one noticed for weeks
findings.summary_md: The Register reported on September 1, 2026 that an attacker stole an API key belonging to AI testing organization METR and consumed roughly $600,000 worth of model credits over several weeks before anyone noticed. Okta's September 9 report cites this case, alongside a $25,000 bill at a software firm and Unit 42's near-million-dollar response cases, as evidence that stolen AI credentials monetize through the victim's own billing.
